justification: Recording rationale for non-applicable provisions (303645) and documenting use of poorly-secured external models (304223) both require justification documentation.
Recording justifications for unmet recommendations and risk-assessing external components are distinct steps of one documented risk management process.
Recording justifications for non-applied provisions (303645) overlaps with maintaining clear audit trail of system design (304223).
Both mandate structured records kept for later scrutiny, but for different purposes: unmet provisions for assurance assessors, data provenance for tracing poisoning.
Recording justifications for unmet recommendations is unrelated to supporting users through an incident.
Credential uniqueness and protection of sensitive data are distinct objectives that jointly prevent unauthorized access to what the system holds.
M2M auth-via-PSK guidance (303645) complements AI access control framework securing APIs/models (304223).
Cryptographic strength of authentication versus the risk of models carrying unused functionality.
Authentication cryptography versus component justification.
Changing an authentication value versus internal channels for disseminating threat updates to staff.
303645 requires simple credential change UI; 304223 requires accessible end-user guidance. Together they ensure users can manage AI/IoT auth.
Brute-force resistance versus continuous infrastructure risk review.
Both mandate brute-force/abuse mitigation: 303645 on device auth, 304223 via API rate limiting against reverse engineering and poisoning.
Both call for analysis of collected telemetry/logs for security anomalies. Same security objective.
Erasure capability and disclosure of how data is used are different obligations that together form user control over personal data.
Both mandate secure removal of data assets; A user data on the device at the user's request, B training data and models at transfer of ownership.
Deletion of personal data from services versus risk from superfluous model capability.
Deletion of personal data from services versus advance notice of model updates.
Personal data deletion from associated services (303645) maps to secure data disposal at end-of-life (304223).
Both mandate secure deletion of data; A on user request, B at decommissioning, each specifying obligations the other omits.
303645 addresses secure installation and maintenance usability; 304223 addresses human oversight of AI systems. The human-factor theme is too general to count as a compliance relationship.
Minimizing security decisions asked of the user and explaining security updates clearly are different obligations serving usable security.
User setup guidance versus assurance over external risk owners.
Setup guidance for consumers versus access protection for training and test data.
Setup guidance versus vulnerability disclosure policy.
User setup guidance versus supply chain process.
Secure setup guidance and transparency about data handling pursue different objectives.
Both give users actionable security information; A guidance for checking secure state, B threat descriptions with recommended actions.
User-side checking and operator-side continuous monitoring are different obligations that together keep a deployed system in a secure state.
Both verify that a deployed system actually carries its intended security controls; A through user-facing checks, B through developer verification.
User guidance on secure state is unrelated to contractual flow-down to cloud providers.
Both require security-relevant information to be documented for those operating the product; A as user guidance, B as system documentation content.
Guidance on checking secure state is unrelated to asset disposal at transfer of ownership.
Input validation is unrelated to threat modelling triggered by configuration change.
UI-level input validation (303645) overlaps with input checks/sanitization for AI models (304223).
Input validation and due diligence on external components pursue different objectives.
Input validation versus disaster recovery planning.
Network-interface input validation (303645) overlaps with sanitization checks on data/inputs (304223).
Input validation and asset disposal at transfer of ownership are unrelated controls.
An inbound disclosure route and outbound communication of unresolved threats are the two directions of one external security communication capability.
Both mandate publication of a clear, accessible vulnerability disclosure policy. Identical security objective.

303645 requires publishing a vulnerability disclosure policy (one specific process for receiving and acknowledging external vulnerability reports); 304223 requires a full AI incident management plan covering disclosure, detection, response, containment, recovery, and communication. The AI provision subsumes VDP as one component of a comprehensive incident management regime.
Both make security documentation available to others, but the disclosure policy and the design audit trail serve different assurance purposes.
Publishing a disclosure policy and recording training data provenance pursue different objectives.
Vulnerability disclosure policy versus preview access that lets operators evaluate model changes.
Timely remediation and staff threat awareness training are different obligations on different parties.
B's audit trail names post-deployment maintenance, the record against which A's documented remediation process operates.
Timely remediation of disclosed vulnerabilities versus audit logging of prompt and configuration changes.
Acting on disclosed vulnerabilities and planning for the unpatchable case cover the two outcomes of a vulnerability report.

303645 requires manufacturers to continually monitor, identify and rectify security vulnerabilities within product components; 304223 requires continuously monitoring the entire system infrastructure AND supply chain AND third-party components for security issues. The AI provision subsumes and extends the IoT requirement — both cover component vulnerability monitoring, but AI also covers supply chain, infrastructure, and third-party dependencies.
Vulnerability monitoring is unrelated to technical measures supporting human oversight.
Vulnerability rectification depends on knowing which assets and versions are deployed, which is what B mandates.
Vulnerability monitoring and incident/recovery planning are separate processes that jointly make up post-market security response.
Finding and fixing vulnerabilities and supporting affected users through an incident are separate parts of one response capability.
Both address remediation of vulnerabilities in fielded products; A the monitoring and rectification, B the provision and delivery of the resulting patches.
Monitoring and rectifying vulnerabilities and planning for when they cannot be fixed are distinct halves of lifecycle vulnerability management.
Continuous vulnerability monitoring and re-testing after a major version change are distinct assurance activities over a product's life.
Updateability of software components versus disaster recovery planning.
Both keep a product securable over its life across the updateable/not-updateable split; A mandates updateability, B mandates contingency where it is impossible.
Both govern how software change is handled safely, A by requiring components to be securely updateable, B by re-testing after a major change.
Update-integrity verification and general resilience to adversarial input are separate objectives that together harden the system against tampering.
A is a specific update-integrity control, B the threat-modelling process that would identify the need for such controls; distinct objectives, jointly effective.
Cryptographic verification of the delivered update and advance notice to users are distinct duties in one update process.
Distributing updates and verifying them on receipt are distinct obligations on different parties in one update chain.
Informing the user that an update is needed versus technical measures supporting human oversight of a model.
Notifying a user of a pending update differs from publishing a policy for receiving vulnerability reports.
Informing end users of a required update versus passing test findings to operators.
Both require informing users of security updates with risk/explanation in an accessible/recognizable way.
Notifying users of a required update versus supporting them through an incident.
A requires informing the user that an update is needed; B covers producing the update, notifying operators, and delivering it to end-users, which includes A's notification duty.
Disruption notification versus configuration audit logging.
User notification of disruptive updates versus use of independent security testers.
Support period publication versus supplier due diligence.
Publishing a support period differs from providing operators preview access to evaluate model changes.
Publishing replacement support versus secure coding training for developers.
Both require the justification documentation to reach users in an accessible way; A specifies its content, B the act of sharing it.
Both require accessible user-facing documentation about the product's lifecycle and use.
Both pursue user-facing transparency about update status; A covers devices that receive none, B covers those that do.
Both address what to do when updates cannot be provided — 303645 publishes rationale, 304223 mandates contingency plans.
Isolability of non-updatable devices versus human oversight of AI systems.
Isolability of a non-updatable device versus documentation of training data sources.
Recognizable device designation and a maintained asset inventory are the outward and inward halves of asset identification.
Presence of a secure update mechanism versus secure coding training.
Both handle the case where a preferred control cannot be applied: A carves out the constrained device, B requires compensating controls and risk assessment.

303645 mandates a secure update mechanism for ALL software components (mandatory, universal); 304223 only addresses how major updates should be treated (as a new model version). The IoT universal update-mechanism requirement subsumes the AI major-update handling procedure — the AI provision covers a specific subset of update scenarios that IoT already governs broadly.
Automatic update activation versus assurance over external risk owners.
Update activation and recovery is unrelated to logging configuration and prompt changes.
Automatic update activation versus guidance on model limitations.
Auto-secure-update at init is a specific delivery mechanism for the regular updates 304223 mandates.
Both require contingency for the case where an update cannot be applied; A through recovery to a known good state, B through documented mitigation plans.
Checking for available updates is unrelated to verifying that specified security controls were implemented.
User control over automatic updates versus awareness of prohibited use cases.
User control over automatic updates versus sharing test findings with operators.
User control over auto-updates (303645) complements end-user configuration guidance (304223).
Both concern dissemination of security update information, but to different audiences: end-user notification control versus internal staff awareness channels.
Update notification preferences versus threat modelling on configuration change.
User control over update notifications versus protection of sensitive training data.
Both concern notifying users about updates; A the user's control over receiving notifications, B the duty to notify before updating.
User control over update notifications is unrelated to contingency planning where updates cannot be provided.
Update cryptography versus matching usage to data sensitivity.
Update timeliness and staff awareness training are unrelated obligations.
Timeliness of security updates versus due diligence on external components.
Timeliness of security updates versus threat modelling on configuration change.
Patching promptly and communicating threats that cannot be patched are distinct duties within one vulnerability handling process.
Releasing fixes promptly and testing releases before shipping are distinct duties in one secure release process.
Prompt patching and support to affected users during an incident are different obligations under one response capability.
303645: device verifies update authenticity/integrity; 304223: developer releases cryptographic hashes for verification. Same crypto-integrity goal.
Verifying an update artefact on receipt and re-testing the system after a major change are distinct assurance steps around one update.
Both require protection of sensitive credentials/weights at rest; 303645 generic CSPs, 304223 model weights/training data.
Both limit exposure of sensitive internals but by different means: protected storage versus evaluating outputs for leakage.
Secure storage of parameters versus evaluating outputs for unintended influence.
Secure storage of security parameters versus guidance on model limitations.
Tamper resistance of a device identity is unrelated to external component due diligence.
Tamper resistance of a device identity is unrelated to permission scoping between systems.
Both defend against reverse engineering of an interface: A by keeping credentials out of the binary, B by limiting abuse of the exposed API.
Prohibiting hard-coded security parameters versus an audit log of configuration changes.
Uniqueness of security parameters versus a threat modelling process naming data poisoning, model inversion and membership inference.
Both govern the credentials and controls protecting access to system assets; A mandates per-device uniqueness, B mandates evaluation of the access control framework.
Both enable authenticity verification of distributed software artefacts; A by unique per-device parameters, B by published cryptographic hashes.
Key uniqueness and post-incident user support share no objective.
Providing updates and holding unique keys with which their authenticity can be checked are distinct parts of one secure update chain.
Best-practice cryptography for secure comms (303645) is a key control under AI infrastructure access framework (304223).
Cryptography for secure communication versus secure software supply chain processes.
Cryptography for secure communication versus security testing before release.
Vetted implementations versus role-tailored security training.
Both demand assurance over externally sourced components before use; A by requiring reviewed implementations, B by requiring risk assessment and due diligence.
Both require verification that security functionality is correctly implemented, A through reviewed implementations and B through checking specified controls were built in.
Vetted cryptographic implementations versus data and input sanitisation.
Both require assurance before release, A that implementations have been reviewed or evaluated, B that the system was security tested.
Reviewed cryptographic implementations versus security update delivery.
Vetted cryptographic implementations versus monitoring internal model states.
Replaceability of cryptographic primitives versus sharing test findings with operators.
Authentication before network access versus maintaining an audit trail over models and datasets.
Authentication on network interfaces (303645) overlaps with API/model access control (304223).

303645 requires authentication for ALL network interface access in the initialized state; 304223 requires controls on external API access specifically to prevent exploitation of ML limitations. IoT's blanket network authentication requirement is broader — every scenario governed by the AI external-API control is a specific instance of the IoT network-authentication mandate, but IoT covers far more network access types.
Both restrict privileged access to system interfaces; A gates configuration behind authentication, B limits inter-system permissions to what functionality requires.
Authentication on a configuration interface versus confidentiality of training and test data; different assets.
Authenticated configuration change versus performance monitoring.

303645 requires critical security parameters to be encrypted in transit with appropriate technology; 304223 requires ALL parties to protect ALL sensitive data including training data, test sets, personal data, and model weights. The AI sensitive-data protection mandate is broader — it covers all data classes at rest and in transit, whereas IoT's requirement is limited to CSPs in transit specifically.
Critical security parameter lifecycle management is a different objective from threat modelling triggered by configuration changes, and B's process text does not name key management.
Both protect security-critical assets; A over the lifecycle of critical security parameters, B through access-control measures on APIs, models and data.
Supply chain process requirements do not name key or parameter management, which is the whole subject of A.
Lifecycle CSP management (303645) and audit trail of system design/maintenance (304223) both support secure lifecycle governance.
Both govern secure handling of sensitive assets across their lifecycle, including disposal; A for critical security parameters, B for training data and models on transfer.
Both apply minimization to unnecessary capability; A disables unused interfaces, B requires the risk of superfluous model functionality to be managed.
Disabling unused interfaces (303645) and access control framework (304223) jointly reduce attack surface.
Limiting interface disclosure is unrelated to external component due diligence.
Both apply minimization at a system boundary; A to the security information disclosed, B to the permissions granted.
Limiting unauthenticated disclosure over network interfaces versus documenting training data provenance.

303645 requires minimizing unauthorized disclosure of ALL security-relevant information on network interfaces; 304223 requires evaluating model outputs to prevent reverse-engineering of training data and model weights. Every case of AI model-output information leakage is a specific instance of the IoT security-information-minimization requirement, but IoT covers a broader category of security-relevant disclosures.
Minimising unauthenticated disclosure versus monitoring internal model states.
Both reduce risk by removing capability that is not needed, A for exposed physical interfaces and B for superfluous model functionality.
Physical attack surface versus cost-based prioritisation of controls.
Physical interface exposure versus communication of unresolvable threats downstream.
Both limit how much of the system an outsider can reach and abuse, A through physical interfaces and B through API access controls.
Physical interface exposure versus mitigating controls around poorly secured third-party components.
Physical interface exposure versus provenance documentation for public training data.
Physical attack surface versus action logging.
Disabled debug interfaces (303645) and dedicated dev environments with separation (304223) both isolate development from production.
Debug port protection versus user guidance.
Disabling unnecessary services versus a threat modelling process naming AI-specific attacks.
Restricting the product technically to its intended use and telling users which uses are prohibited are the technical and informational halves of scope enforcement.
Enabling only required services versus component justification.
Disabling unnecessary services versus guidance on appropriate use and failure modes.
Code minimization versus assurance that an external risk owner can address its risks.
Least-privilege software (303645) and least-privilege permissions for AI system to other systems (304223) — same principle.
Least privilege versus cost-based prioritisation of identified risks.
Hardware mitigation of memory exploits and training that stops such flaws being written are distinct measures against one exploitation route.
Hardware memory access control versus maintaining an audit trail.
Memory access control versus incident management and recovery planning.
Securing one's own development process and assessing externally sourced components are distinct duties that together determine the security of the delivered software.
A secure development process and the specific obligation to strip superfluous model capability both fall under secure development of the artefact.
Secure development processes versus technical measures supporting human oversight.
Both aim at security being correctly built into the delivered software, A through development process and B through verification of specified controls.
Both mandate secure software development processes including version control; A adds compiler hardening for device software, B adds asset tracking and authentication for AI assets.
Secure development of one's own software versus re-evaluating third-party released models.
Version control of artefacts and publication of hashes that let recipients verify them are two halves of artefact integrity.
Both require changes to a system to be tracked, A through version control in development and B through an audit log of configuration and prompt changes.
Secure development practice and pre-deployment testing are different objectives that jointly govern a secure release.

303645 requires software integrity verification using secure boot and hardware root of trust (a specific integrity control at boot time); 304223 requires following secure software supply chain processes covering model development, procurement, third-party components, and ongoing integrity across the full lifecycle. The AI supply chain security requirement subsumes the IoT boot-integrity check as one element of a broader, end-to-end software integrity mandate.
Secure boot verification versus evaluating outputs for unintended influence over the system.
Alerting on software tampering versus the risk of unused model capability.
Alerting on detected software tampering versus awareness of prohibited use cases.
Tamper alerting on the device versus contractual arrangements with cloud operators.

303645 requires alerting on detected unauthorized changes to device software; 304223 requires logging ALL system and user actions to support compliance, incident investigations, and vulnerability tracking. The AI logging mandate is broader — it captures all actions proactively for multiple purposes (compliance, forensics, incident response), whereas IoT logs only in reaction to detected unauthorized changes.
Unauthorized change detection is unrelated to asset disposal at transfer of ownership.
Cryptographic confidentiality in transit versus least-privilege permissions between systems.
Transport encryption and asset tracking processes share no objective.
Confidentiality of personal data in transit (303645) and protection of sensitive data including training/test (304223) — same goal across data types.
Encryption of personal data in transit versus the security content of model documentation.
Sensitive personal data crypto protection (303645) maps to AI sensitive-data protection (304223).

303645 mandates (SHALL) cryptographic protection for ALL sensitive personal data communicated between device and services; 304223 requires proportionate protection (conditional: 'where...could be confidential') for training data and model weights. IoT's requirement is mandatory and covers all sensitive personal data in transit; AI's is conditional and scoped to model-specific confidential assets.
Both protect data assets from unauthorized access; A through transport encryption, B through evaluation of the access control framework.
Encryption of sensitive personal data in transit versus accessible user guidance on system configuration.
Encryption of sensitive personal data in transit versus the delivery chain for security patches.

303645 discloses external sensing capabilities to end-users for privacy transparency; 304223 requires developers to maintain an internal audit trail of ML data preparation. Different audience (consumer vs. developer), subject (device sensors vs. ML data lineage), and purpose.
Documenting external sensing capabilities (303645) overlaps with conveying data usage/access/storage to end-users (304223).
Resilience to network and power outage versus monitoring internal model states.
Stable network connection state (303645) complements broader AI disaster recovery planning (304223).
Orderly network reconnection versus monitoring model behaviour for security-relevant drift.
